content: Osha, scientifically known as Ligusticum porteri, is a perennial herb that has been traditionally utilized for its medicinal properties. This plant is native to certain regions of the Rocky Mountains, particularly in the southwestern areas of North America. The root of Ligusticum porteri (osha) or Ligusticum wallichii can be prepared by steeping it in ethanol-based solutions, such as whiskey or vodka, for a minimum duration of one month. The resulting tincture, while pungent in aroma, serves as an effective liniment for alleviating sore muscles. When stored in a cool environment, this tincture can be preserved indefinitely. Osha is known by a variety of alternative names, including but not limited to: Osha root, Porter’s Lovage, Porter’s Licorice-root, Lovage, Wild Lovage, Porter’s Wild Lovage, Loveroot, Porter’s Ligusticum, Bear Medicine, Bear Root, Colorado Cough Root, Indian Root, Indian Parsley, Wild Parsley, Mountain Ginseng, Mountain Carrot, Nipo, Empress of the Dark Forest, Chuchupate, Chuchupati, Chuchupaste, Chuchupatle, Guariaca, Hierba del cochino, Raíz del cochino, Washía (in the Tarahumara language), and Yerba de cochino. In the Jicarilla language, it is referred to as ha’ich’idéé, while the White Mountain Apache people call it Ha’ilchii’gah. Osha continues to be widely used by the Apache and other Native American tribes. According to White Mountain Apache elders, the herb was traditionally employed as a repellent against snakes and insects due to its strong odor. Additionally, the Apache people have used osha to treat ailments such as the common cold, sore throats, coughs, sinusitis, and other respiratory conditions often associated with the winter season. It is also believed that placing osha in water and allowing it to simmer on a wood stove can help bolster immunity during the colder months.
